newsitem.title: KENYA: Violence at Kenyan opposition rally, man killed.
newsitem.headline: Violence at Kenyan opposition rally, man killed.

text.p: A man suspected of being a police spy was beaten to death at an opposition rally in Nairobi on Friday and several hundred opposition supporters took to the streets to press demands for constitutional reforms.
Barely 1,000 activists turned up for the rally in Nairobi's Uhuru park to hear opposition speakers demand sweeping political reforms from President Daniel arap Moi before elections due this year.
Said Athman, a spokesman for the medical charity St Johns, told Reuters a man identified as Gilbert Ahanya Simiyu was pronounced dead on arrival at Nairobi hospital at around noon (0900 GMT).
Witnesses said Simiyu was beaten by a mob shortly after the rally started. Oppostion supporters said he was from the police special branch division. Police could not confirm or deny the report.
Two other people were also attacked and beaten but they fled and were not in serious physical danger, witnesses said.
At the end of the rally, several hundred supporters of a one-day general strike in Kenya took to the city centre, breaking shop windows and chanting slogans against Moi, witnesses said.
They said the youths rampaged through the city centre and stoned some buses and cars.
"They are now breaking into shops. They are setting up barricades and blocking traffic," a Reuters correspondent at the scene said.

Heavily armed police and units of the feared paramilitary General Service Unit moved in and fired in the air to disperse the demonstrators. Witnesses said order was swiftly restored in the city centre.

Most city centre shops were closed and some workers stayed at home. But shop-owners, many from the vulnerable Asian community, said they closed for fear of the violence and looting which mar political demonstrations in Kenya.
The national strike and protest marches called by the fragmented opposition had scant success and Kenya's battered currency recouped some of its losses.
Moi's government declared the strike and planned rallies unlawful but security forces allowed the Nairobi meeting to go ahead without disruption.
The port of Mombasa, the East African country's second city, was calm with only a few shops closed, residents said.
Tension has risen steadily in the past two months and at least nine people were killed on July 7 when security forces suppressed pro-reform protests in Nairobi and other centres.
The shilling sank to an historic official low against the dollar on Thursday but regained 1.85 percent by about midday on Friday, standing at a commercial mean of 68.06 to the dollar.

But traders said the currency was still fragile and it was too soon to talk of a recovery. The shilling has lost nearly 16 percent since the International Monetary Fund (IMF) shelved a $205 million loan last week because of concerns over official corruption.
Now aged 73 and in power since 1978, Moi wants a final five-year term. Under pressure at home and from Western donors, he has assented to some reforms before the polls.
This concession has successfully deepened the divisions within the opposition and two prominent leaders, Kenneth Matiba and Kijana Wamalwa, opposed Friday's strike.
Work went on almost as normal in Nairobi's industrial area, one employer said.
"We are open. Almost everybody -- about 180 of my 200 employees -- turned up," bed and mattress manufacturer Mahedi Meghji told Reuters.

The strike and marches in Nairobi and 11 provincial towns were called by the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), an umbrella reform group which wants sweeping changes to the constitution and the repeal of numerous laws before the elections.
